At deeper cutoffs, 76.3% and 65.0% achieved uMRD (<10−5) and uMRD (<10−6) with VenO, respectively, vs 43.0% and 25.6% with FCR/BR.

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: The phase 3 CRISTALLO trial compared first-line fixed-duration venetoclax-obinutuzumab (VenO) vs fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, and rituximab (FCR)/bendamustine-rituximab (BR) in patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), using undetectable minimal residual disease (uMRD) as the sole primary end point. Previously untreated patients with a cumulative illness rating scale score ≤6 and creatinine clearance ≥70 mL/min without del(17p)/TP53 mutations were randomized 1:1 to VenO or FCR/BR. The primary end point was uMRD (<10−4) in peripheral blood (PB) using next-generation sequencing at month 15. Key secondary end points included uMRD (<10−4) in PB and bone marrow (BM) at end of treatment (EOT) and progression-free survival (PFS). uMRD at deeper cutoffs were explored. At data cutoff (19 March 2024), 80 patients received VenO, and 86 received FCR/BR. Baseline characteristics were generally balanced across arms. The primary end point was met: 81.3% (VenO) and 54.7% (FCR/BR) achieved uMRD (<10−4) in PB at month 15 (P = .0004). uMRD (<10−4) in PB and BM at EOT was also higher with VenO vs FCR/BR. Short follow-up precluded evaluation of PFS at the first planned interim analysis; however, fewer patients progressed/died with VenO vs FCR/BR (7 vs 13). At month 15, 65.0% (VenO) and 25.6% (FCR/BR) achieved uMRD (<10−6) in PB. The overall safety profile was consistent with the known safety profile of each drug. No patient in the VenO arm was deemed high risk for tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) after obinutuzumab debulking; no clinical TLS occurred. These results confirm and extend the findings from the GAIA-CLL13 trial, validating increased depth of response with VenO vs chemoimmunotherapies. This trial was registered at www.clinicaltrials.gov as NCT04285567.

The disease course of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is heterogeneous but typically is long, and traditional end points for trials such as progression-free survival and overall survival are increasingly unrealistic for drug development when most patients do well. Sharman et al report on the results of the first randomized study of treatment-naive CLL that used undetectable minimal residual disease as the sole primary end point, proving the superiority of venetoclax plus obinutuzumab (VenO) over older standard chemoimmunotherapy regimens by 15 months with this surrogate end point. Longer follow-up could well validate this end point for first-line treatments in future registration trials.

sec.p: Received 2025 Jul 25; Accepted 2026 Feb 9; Issue date 2026 Jun 11.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Approved first-line treatments for patients with chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) include fixed-duration chemoimmunotherapy1; a Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor (BTKi) as continuous therapy2; venetoclax, a B-cell lymphoma 2 inhibitor, in combination with obinutuzumab, an anti-CD20 antibody, as fixed-duration therapy3; and a BTKi in combination with venetoclax.4, 5, 6

Achieving undetectable minimal residual disease (uMRD) below reliable limits of detection, such as <1 CLL cell per 10 000 leukocytes (<10−4), using sensitive techniques including flow cytometry, allele-specific oligonucleotide polymerase chain reaction, and next-generation sequencing (NGS), can be a strong independent predictor of progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) after fixed-duration CLL therapy.7, 8, 9, 10, 11 In the CLL14 phase 3 trial, uMRD rates were durable and predictive of PFS after first-line venetoclax-obinutuzumab (VenO) treatment in patients with CLL.12 The correlation between uMRD and prolonged survival outcomes have also been observed with nonvenetoclax regimens, such as fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, and rituximab (FCR), bendamustine-rituximab (BR), and obinutuzumab-chlorambucil.13, 14, 15 A meta-analysis demonstrated that MRD is an appropriate primary end point in CLL trials of chemoimmunotherapy.16 Despite evidence supporting uMRD as a surrogate end point for PFS in CLL, it has not been used as a standalone primary end point in clinical trials; the phase 3 GAIA-CLL13 trial used uMRD (<10−4) in peripheral blood (PB) using flow cytometry as a coprimary end point.17

Here, we present results from the primary analysis of the CRISTALLO phase 3 trial (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04285567), comparing first-line VenO and FCR/BR in fit patients without del17p or TP53 mutations, using uMRD (<10−4) measured by NGS as the sole primary end point.

sec.title: Study design
sec.p: CRISTALLO is an open-label, international, multicenter, randomized phase 3 trial investigating the efficacy and safety of VenO vs FCR/BR in fit patients with previously untreated CLL. Patients aged ≥18 years, with a cumulative illness rating scale score ≤6, creatinine clearance ≥70 mL/min, without del(17p) or TP53 mutations, and in need of treatment (according to the International Workshop on CLL guidelines18) were eligible. Only patients aged ≤65 years were eligible for FCR following treatment recommendations (based on treatment-related toxicity and availability of alternative protocols).

Patients were randomized 1:1 to receive VenO or FCR/BR. Patients in the VenO arm received fixed-duration treatment for twelve 28-day cycles. In cycle 1, 1000 mg IV obinutuzumab was administered on day 1 (or as a split dose across day 1/2), day 8, and day 15, as well as day 1 of cycles 2 to 6. Venetoclax was initiated with a 5-week ramp-up period on cycle 1 day 22, with administration of 400 mg daily from cycles 3 to 12. Patients in the FCR/BR arm received either 6 cycles of FCR (25 mg/m2 fludarabine IV and 250 mg/m2 cyclophosphamide IV on days 1-3 of each 28-day cycle; and rituximab IV on day 1 of each cycle [375 mg/m2 in cycle 1 and 500 mg/m2 in cycles 2-6]) or 6 cycles of BR (90 mg/m2 bendamustine IV on day 1 and day 2 of each 28-day cycle and rituximab IV on day 1 for each cycle (375 mg/m2 in cycle 1 and 500 mg/m2 in cycles 2-6). Randomization was stratified according to Binet stage (A, B, or C), immunoglobulin heavy-chain variable region gene (IGHV) mutational status, and age (≤65 or >65 years).

sec.title: Assessments and end points
sec.p: Efficacy analyses were conducted in the intent-to-treat population. The primary end point was uMRD rate, defined as the proportion of patients achieving uMRD (<1 CLL cell in 10 000 leukocytes; <10−4) in PB using NGS at month 15 (assay described in the supplemental Methods available on the Blood website). Key secondary efficacy end points were uMRD (<10−4) rates in PB and bone marrow (BM) at end of treatment (EOT; 8-12 weeks after the last VenO dose [∼15 months from first dose] or 8-12 weeks after the last FCR/BR dose [∼9 months from first dose]) and investigator-assessed PFS. Scheduling of MRD assessment in PB and BM are shown in supplemental Figure 1. Other secondary and exploratory end points, including uMRD rates at deeper cutoffs (<10−5 and <10−6) and longitudinal MRD modeling, are described in the supplemental Methods.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: uMRD rates across both arms were compared using the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test, stratified by Binet stage, IGHV mutational status, and age. Differences in uMRD rates were estimated, and 2-sided 95% Anderson-Hauck confidence intervals (CI) were provided. Within each arm, 2-sided 95% Clopper-Pearson exact CI were also presented. The primary end point was tested at a significance level of 5%. Approximately 165 patients were required to achieve a power of 92%, assuming a target improvement of 30% in uMRD rate (vs an assumed control rate of 52% for FCR/BR). The minimum detectable difference in uMRD rate was 14.1%.

Key secondary end points were formally tested in the following hierarchical order: PFS, uMRD rate in PB at EOT, and uMRD rate in BM at EOT. PFS was analyzed according to the first planned interim analysis (in which ∼25 events [or 57% information fraction] was expected) using O’Brien-Fleming boundaries for statistical significance. Comparison of PFS was performed using a 2-sided log-rank test at an overall significance level of 0.05, adjusted for the interim analysis, using Kaplan-Meier methodology and adjusted for the stratification factors previously mentioned. Estimates of the treatment effects on PFS were expressed as hazard ratios (HR) using a stratified Cox proportional-hazards analysis, including 95% CI.

For the key secondary end points of uMRD rates in PB and BM at EOT, the same statistical method for the primary end point was adopted. However, due to the hierarchical testing procedure in place, uMRD rates in PB and BM at EOT could not be considered statistically significant until PFS reached statistical significance. For the remaining secondary end points, no α-controlled rules were in place; thus, they were not considered confirmatory (descriptive P values were provided).

This study was conducted in full conformance with the International Council for Harmonisation of Technical Requirements for Pharmaceuticals for Human Use E6 guideline for Good Clinical Practice and the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki or the applicable laws and regulations of the country in which the research is conducted, whichever affords the greater protection to the individual. All patients provided written informed consent, and patients were able to withdraw their consent at any time for any reason.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Patients were enrolled from 28 May 2020 to 23 January 2023. At data cutoff when all patients reached month 15 (19 March 2024), 80 patients were randomized to VenO and 86 to FCR/BR (Figure 1). Baseline demographics and clinical characteristics were generally balanced (Table 1). In the VenO and FCR/BR arms, the median age was 62 (range, 40-83) vs 61 years (range, 36-77), 28 of 80 (35.0%) vs 29 of 86 (33.7%) were aged >65 years, 55 of 80 (68.8%) vs 57 of 86 (66.3%) were male, and 44 of 80 (55.0%) vs 49 of 86 (57.0%) had mutated IGHV, respectively. Overall, 49.4% (VenO, n = 40/80; FCR/BR, n = 42/86) had Binet stage B disease, 37.3% had stage C (VenO, n = 33/80; FCR/BR, n = 29/86), and 11.4% had stage A (VenO, n = 7/80; FCR/BR, n = 12/86).

sec.p: Overall, 78.8% completed VenO, 83.8% completed 12 cycles of venetoclax, and 75.6% completed FCR/BR. Reasons for early discontinuation for each study drug are outlined in supplemental Table 1. The median duration of follow-up was 31.6 months.

sec.title: Primary end point and key secondary end points
sec.p: At the primary analysis, the primary end point was met: 81.3% of patients treated with VenO achieved uMRD (<10−4) in PB at month 15 vs 54.7% with FCR/BR (difference, 26.6 [95% CI, 12.3-40.9]; P = .0004; Figure 2). These results were consistent across baseline demographics and clinical characteristics subgroups, including those defined by IGHV mutation status (supplemental Figures 2 and 3). uMRD (<10−4) rates in PB at EOT were also higher with VenO vs FCR/BR (81.3% vs 60.5%; difference, 20.8 [95% CI, 6.7-34.9]; P = .0053). Similarly, uMRD (<10−4) rates in BM at EOT were higher with VenO vs FCR/BR (70.0% vs 38.4%; difference, 31.6 [95% CI, 16.6-46.7]; P < .0001). Overall, there was high concordance between uMRD (<10−4) rates in PB and BM at EOT (82.7%).

sec.p: At data cutoff, the key secondary end point of PFS was not met at the first planned interim analysis due to the short survival follow-up. Fewer patients experienced a PFS event with VenO (7/80 [8.8%]; 3 died [2 due to COVID-19 pneumonia and 1 due to pneumonia] and 4 progressed) vs FCR/BR (13/86 [15.1%]; 3 died [COVID-19, COVID-19 pneumonia, and sepsis] and 10 progressed; HR, 0.49; 95% CI, 0.2-1.3; P = .13; Figure 3); 2-year PFS rates were 95.7% and 90.4%, respectively. In patients who progressed with VenO, 3 had achieved uMRD (<10−4) at EOT, but none reached deeper cutoffs (<10−6). All 10 patients who progressed with FCR/BR were MRD positive.

sec.title: Other secondary end points
sec.p: Overall response rate (ORR) was numerically higher with VenO vs FCR/BR (88.8% vs 79.1%; P = .1119; supplemental Table 2). In the VenO arm, 40 of 80 (50.0%) achieved complete response (CR)/CR with incomplete blood count recovery (CRi). In the FCR/BR arm, fewer patients (28/86 [32.6%]) achieved CR/CRi. In patients with CR/CRi at month 15, uMRD (<10−4) rate in PB was higher with VenO vs FCR/BR (39/40 [97.5%] vs 22/28 [78.6%]; P = .0054). In these patients, uMRD (<10−4) rate in BM at EOT was also higher with VenO vs FCR/BR (35/40 [87.5%] vs 17/28 [60.7%]; P = .0038).

Median duration of overall response was not reached for either arm (supplemental Figure 4). A trend for event-free survival benefit was observed with VenO vs FCR/BR; 8.8% of patients died (n = 3) or progressed (n = 4) with VenO, whereas 18.6% of patients died (n = 3), progressed (n = 9), or initiated new anti-CLL treatment (n = 4) with FCR/BR (HR, 0.41; 95% CI, 0.17-1.01; P = .045; supplemental Figure 5). At this cutoff, OS data were immature; 3 patients in each arm had died (VenO [COVID-19 pneumonia, n = 2; pneumonia, n = 1]; FCR/BR [COVID-19, COVID-19 pneumonia, and sepsis, n = 1 each]). Median OS was not reached for either arm (supplemental Figure 6).

At baseline, of the 80 patients in the VenO arm, 11 (13.8%), 50 (62.5%), and 19 patients (23.8%) were deemed as low, medium, and high risk for tumor lysis syndrome (TLS), respectively. After 3 doses of obinutuzumab debulking, 57 of the 69 patients who were at medium and high risk at baseline achieved TLS risk reduction before venetoclax initiation (Figure 4). Of the 19 high-risk patients at baseline, 2 withdrew from the study before venetoclax initiation (1 withdrew after 3 doses of obinutuzumab, whereas the other discontinued after enrollment before receiving any treatment due to an adverse event [AE]); the remaining 17 patients had reduced TLS risk before venetoclax treatment. Per the venetoclax label, patients deemed high risk should be hospitalized for the initiation of the 20- and 50-mg venetoclax doses. Thus, for 17 high-risk patients, a total of 34 nights of mandatory hospitalization would be required for TLS monitoring during the venetoclax ramp-up period; however, after obinutuzumab, no patients who initiated venetoclax were high risk, and therefore 0 nights were mandated in hospital.

caption.p: Sankey plot of TLS risk at baseline and at reassessment after 3 doses of obinutuzumab in the VenO arm (ITT population). TLS risk reassessment was conducted at cycle 1 day 22 (or cycle 1 days 16-21).

sec.title: Exploratory end points
sec.p: In PB, the duration of uMRD (<10−4), measured by NGS, was sustained over time, and the depth of response was greater with VenO vs FCR/BR (Figure 5). At deeper cutoffs, 76.3% and 65.0% of patients in the VenO arm achieved uMRD (<10−5) and uMRD (<10−6) in PB at month 15, respectively, vs 43.0% and 25.6% of patients in the FCR/BR arm (supplemental Table 3). Similarly, 58.8% and 32.5% of patients in the VenO arm achieved uMRD (<10−5) and uMRD (<10−6) in BM at EOT, respectively, vs 30.2% and 15.1% of patients in the FCR/BR arm (supplemental Table 4). Across all uMRD cutoffs, the proportion of patients achieving uMRD was higher with VenO vs FCR vs BR both in PB at month 15 (81.3% vs 65.2% vs 44.7% at <10−4; supplemental Table 3) and BM at EOT (70.0% vs 52.2% vs 23.7% at <10−4; supplemental Table 4). The proportion of patients achieving uMRD (<10−6) was also higher with VenO vs FCR vs BR, both in PB at month 15 (65.0% vs 37.0% vs 13.2%) and BM at EOT (32.5% vs 19.6% vs 10.5%). Kinetic analyses also demonstrated that the uMRD rates were consistently deeper with VenO irrespective of IGHV subgroups, and this was maintained in subsequent treatment cycles beyond month 15 (supplemental Figure 3). Additionally, among patients with mutated IGHV, the number of PFS events was 2 in the VenO arm vs 3 in the FCR/BR arm; all 3 PFS events in the FCR/BR arm were in patients who received treatment with BR only. ORR was higher with VenO (88.8%) vs FCR (82.6%) vs BR (78.9%); the proportion of patients achieving CR was also higher with VenO vs FCR vs BR (supplemental Table 2). Patients who failed to achieve uMRD with FCR/BR appeared to have poorer PFS outcomes vs those achieving uMRD with FCR/BR. No PFS difference was observed between patients failing to achieve uMRD and those achieving uMRD in the VenO arm. Among MRD-positive patients, VenO may be associated with better outcomes than FCR/BR (supplemental Figure 7). The MRD dynamic model predicted that the median MRD level at EOT was significantly lower after VenO vs after FCR/BR (6.0 × 10−8 vs 3.6 × 10−6, respectively; P < .0001; Figure 6).

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: Safety results in safety-evaluable patients are summarized in Table 2; common AEs (≥10%) are presented in supplemental Table 5. AEs leading to withdrawal of individual study drugs are shown in supplemental Table 6. The most common reasons for serious AEs were events requiring hospitalization or prolonged hospitalization (42/77 [54.5%] and 37/85 [43.5%] with VenO and FCR/BR, respectively). Three patients in each arm died (VenO [COVID-19 pneumonia, n = 2; pneumonia, n = 1]; FCR/BR [COVID-19, COVID-19 pneumonia, and sepsis, n = 1 each]) and were considered unrelated to treatment. No COVID-19 vaccination history was reported for the 2 patients in the VenO arm who died due to COVID-19 pneumonia (1 patient had a history of influenza vaccination, and 1 had a history of pneumococcal vaccination). In the FCR/BR arm, no vaccination history details were reported for the patient who died due to COVID-19 pneumonia, whereas the other patient who died due to COVID-19 had a history of pneumococcal and COVID-19 vaccinations.

sec.p: Laboratory TLS occurred in 8 of 77 patients (10.4%) in the VenO arm; of these, 2 were high risk, and 6 were medium risk at baseline. All events occurred during the first week of obinutuzumab treatment and before venetoclax treatment (none occurred during the venetoclax ramp-up period); 5 patients received treatment for laboratory TLS, 2 had dose modification/interruption, and no patients withdrew from treatment because of TLS. No events were fatal, and all had resolved (median time to resolution, 2 days [range, 1-4]). No clinical TLS occurred.

Overall, 55 of 77 (71.4%) and 51 of 85 patients (60.0%) in the VenO and FCR/BR arms experienced an infection, respectively; of these, 26.0% (20/77) and 24.7% (21/85) were grade ≥3. The most common infections were COVID-19, COVID-19 pneumonia, upper respiratory tract infection, and pneumonia. Hypogammaglobulinemia occurred in 3 patients (2 with VenO [grade 1 and 2] and 1 with FCR/BR [grade 4]). Grade 3 to 4 neutropenia occurred in 42 of 77 patients (54.5%) and 44 of 85 patients (51.8%) in the VenO and FCR/BR arms, respectively; rates were 56.5% (26/46) in patients treated with FCR and 47.4% (18/38) in patients treated with BR. Grade 3 to 4 thrombocytopenia occurred in 23 of 77 (29.9%) and 11 of 85 patients (12.9%) in the VenO and FCR/BR arms, respectively; rates were 15.2% (7/46) in patients treated with FCR and 10.5% (4/38) in patients treated with BR. Overall, 3 patients in the VenO arm and 7 patients in the FCR/BR arm experienced AEs of second primary malignancies (SPMs); none led to dose withdrawal/modification. In the VenO arm, all SPMs were grade 3 and were unresolved/ongoing by data cutoff; 1 patient had a serious SPM event and received treatment. In the FCR/BR arm, 5 were grade 2, and 2 were grade 3. Two cases had not resolved/recovered by data cutoff. Three patients had serious SPM events and received treatment. One event was considered related to treatment. No patients had prior nonmelanoma skin cancer, and no Richter transformation was reported.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: At this primary analysis, the CRISTALLO trial met its primary end point and demonstrated significant improvement in uMRD (<10−4) rate in PB at month 15 with VenO vs FCR/BR in patients with previously untreated CLL. The key secondary efficacy end point of PFS did not reach statistical significance at this interim analysis. Secondary and exploratory uMRD end points were consistent with the primary end point, but due to the hierarchical testing procedure, these were not yet confirmatory. Although exploratory, uMRD and ORR results from the VenO arm demonstrated superiority over FCR alone, suggesting that the observed differences when comparing VenO with the combined FCR/BR arm cannot be driven by BR alone.

The overall safety profile observed was consistent with the known safety profile of each study drug. No new safety concerns for VenO were identified, and the safety profile of VenO continues to be manageable. Most deaths in CRISTALLO, which was conducted in 5 countries during the peak of the COVID-19 pandemic, were COVID-19 related (VenO, 2.5%; FCR/BR, 2.3%). In the AMPLIFY trial, a larger study conducted during a similar period across 27 countries, the incidence of COVID-19 deaths was higher with acalabrutinib-VenO (8.7%) and FCR/BR (7.2%) compared with acalabrutinib-venetoclax (3.4%), suggesting a greater risk of being immunocompromised with anti-CD20–containing regimens.19

Although MRD measurement is an established prognostic tool in CLL, with the European Medicines Agency declaring it a surrogate end point for clinical trials in 2016, to our knowledge, it has not been used as a standalone primary end point. Results from CRISTALLO were consistent with the findings from the corresponding treatment arms in the phase 3 GAIA-CLL13 trial (n = 926), in which the coprimary end point was uMRD (<10−4) in PB at month 15 using flow cytometry: 86.5% vs 52.0% of patients treated with VenO vs FCR/BR achieved uMRD.17 The GAIA-CLL13 trial population was similar to CRISTALLO and was conducted in young (median age, 61 years) and fit patients (cumulative illness rating scale score ≤6; creatinine clearance ≥70 mL/min) without del(17p) or TP53 mutations. Similarly, in the phase 3 CLL14 trial (n = 432), 75.5% vs 35.2% of patients treated with VenO vs chlorambucil-obinutuzumab achieved uMRD (<10−4; assessed by allele-specific oligonucleotide polymerase chain reaction) in PB at month 15.20 In the FLAIR trial of MRD-guided ibrutinib-venetoclax vs FCR, PFS was 97.2% vs 76.8% at 3 years, respectively.21 In the CLL8 trial of FCR vs fludarabine-cyclophosphamide, 68% vs 38% achieved uMRD (<10−4).13 The uMRD (<10−4) rate in the FCR/BR arm in CRISTALLO was lower than those achieved with FCR alone in FLAIR and CLL8, which may be explained by the inclusion of BR. Indeed, when looking at the individual treatments in the FCR/BR arm, the uMRD (<10−4) rate was 65.2% for FCR vs 44.7% for BR in PB at month 15. Additionally, because a higher proportion of patients in the VenO arm achieved lower levels of uMRD (<10−5 and <10−6) vs FCR in CRISTALLO, it will be of great interest to determine the fraction of patients cured by VenO after longer follow-up.

uMRD data are also emerging for fixed-duration venetoclax and BTKi combinations. The CLL17 trial recently showed that uMRD (<10−4) rates were higher with VenO (73.3%) vs ibrutinib-venetoclax (47.2%), and 3-year PFS rates remained similar (81.1% and 79.4%, respectively).22 In the recent AMPLIFY trial of acalabrutinib-venetoclax (with or without obinutuzumab) vs FCR/BR, 8.4%, 70.9%, and 23.7% of patients receiving acalabrutinib-venetoclax, acalabrutinib-VenO, and FCR/BR achieved uMRD (<10−6; assessed by NGS) in PB at EOT, respectively.19 In CRISTALLO, 65.0% achieved uMRD (<10−6) with VenO in PB at month 15. This suggests that acalabrutinib, similar to all BTKis, likely does not primarily drive MRD, either alone or when combined with venetoclax, although it may add benefit when combined with both venetoclax and obinutuzumab. In addition, the GAIA-CLL13 trial demonstrated that BTKis, when given in a triple-combination regimen, may affect PFS despite minimal differences in MRD rates: uMRD (<10−4) rates were 92.2% and 86.5%, whereas 5-year PFS rates were 81.3% and 69.8% for VenO-ibrutinib and VenO, respectively.17,23 The role of BTKis on MRD remains unclear, and there is a need to understand the correlation between MRD and PFS when comparing different partners added to venetoclax.

Importantly, studies have shown that obinutuzumab plays a major role in driving MRD in CLL vs rituximab. The single-arm phase 3b nonrandomized GREEN trial of obinutuzumab plus fludarabine-cyclophosphamide demonstrated MRD-negativity rates of 93.8% in the MRD-evaluable population and 64.3% in the intent-to-treat population in PB.24 In the GAIA-CLL13 trial, uMRD rates with VenO in PB (86.5%) were higher than with venetoclax-rituximab (57.0%).17 Altogether, these reinforce the combination of VenO in achieving high uMRD rates, including at deeper cutoffs in CRISTALLO.

Crosstrial comparisons (particularly when comparing biologically distinct modalities) should be interpreted with caution. Although MRD has long been considered a potential surrogate marker for PFS, recent data from these phase 3 trials, particularly when BTKis are involved, limit the extent that MRD can be extrapolated to predict PFS; therefore, MRD and PFS may be better suited as coprimary end points for these regimens. Despite this, the GAIA-CLL13 trial does suggest that MRD may be predictive of PFS when comparing VenO vs FCR/BR, but longer follow-up is needed in the CRISTALLO trial to draw any conclusions and confirm the suitability of MRD as a primary end point for VenO.

Notably, several challenges need to be addressed before MRD can be used in routine clinical practice, including standardizing the measurement method, defining the ideal MRD compartment (eg, PB vs BM), and how to account for the quality of MRD remission (as particular patient subgroups, eg, high risk, have a shorter time to next treatment). Another important aspect to investigate is whether the depth of response is predictive of duration in patients treated with venetoclax in combination with BTKis or anti-CD20 antibodies. Furthermore, the question remains as to what the best combination partner or optimal duration of therapy is for venetoclax and whether these differ depending on patient population (eg, different age groups and fitness); numerous ongoing clinical trials, including GLOW (NCT03462719), MAJIC (NCT05057494), and CLL16 (NCT05197192), are investigating different venetoclax combinations in patients with previously untreated CLL.

Exploratory analyses demonstrated that the duration of uMRD over time in PB by NGS was supportive of a clinical benefit of VenO. Additionally, obinutuzumab debulking was well tolerated and effective in reducing TLS risk, because no clinical TLS events occurred, most patients in the VenO arm had reduced TLS risk, and no patients remained high risk for TLS when initiating venetoclax; therefore, no patient required mandatory hospitalization. This confirms the manageable safety profile of venetoclax in patients with CLL, provided that debulking, monitoring, and prophylaxis measures are followed.

A limitation of this analyses is the short survival follow-up, which meant PFS did not reach statistical significance at this interim PFS analysis. Based on previous data demonstrating a clear association between MRD and PFS, thereby supporting MRD as a potential surrogate end point, this study was designed with MRD as the sole primary end point, whereas PFS was assessed as a secondary end point to confirm the clinical significance of MRD.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: The CRISTALLO trial demonstrated significant improvement in uMRD (<10−4) rate in PB at month 15 with fixed-duration VenO vs FCR/BR in patients with previously untreated CLL. Results from this trial confirm and extend the findings from the GAIA-CLL13 trial, validating the increased depth of response with VenO vs existing chemoimmunotherapies.
